His scriptorium cell was orderly to a fault; ink pots lined up precisely, quills sharpened to identical points, and parchment stacked in neat, unwavering piles. He took immense pride in his work, the slow, deliberate process of copying the illuminated manuscripts that sustained the monastery of St. Michael. Today’s task was particularly demanding: the *Liber Bestiarum*, a compendium of fantastical creatures, richly adorned with vibrant, if somewhat unsettling, illustrations.

He’d been assigned the chapter describing the Basilisk, a serpent whose gaze could petrify a man. The script was particularly ornate, the lettering tight and elegant, demanding complete concentration. He’d diligently transcribed the text, carefully mimicking the original scribe’s hand, ensuring each flourish and descender was perfect. When the final line – “And its venom doth distill the very marrow from the bones” – was complete, he’d carefully placed the parchment on the drying rack, a narrow ledge running along the back wall of his cell, and secured the scriptorium door as dusk settled.

The scriptorium, like all enclosed spaces within St. Michael’s, was locked and barred from the setting of the sun until the first light of dawn. The practice had been established centuries ago, a safeguard against thieves and vagrants, and a constant reminder of the cloistered life the monks had vowed. It was a system that worked; no breaches had been recorded in living memory. Thomas, like the others, trusted in the ritual.

When he returned to his cell the following morning, a chill prickled his skin that had nothing to do with the early hour. He had fully expected to find the page drying undisturbed, ready for the next stage of illumination. Instead, he found something entirely inexplicable. A new line of text had appeared, scrawled across the bottom of the parchment, in a hand utterly unlike the original, or his own.

The words, penned in a coarse, shaky script, read: "The shadows lengthen, even within stone.” Thomas stared, his breath catching in his throat. He ran a trembling finger over the unfamiliar lettering. The ink was the same as his own – a carefully guarded blend of gall and vitriol, prepared only by the senior monks. There was no other entrance to the scriptorium; the windows were small, high, and sealed. He’d locked the door himself.

He examined the parchment closely, searching for any sign of tampering, any indication of forced entry. Nothing. The text appeared seamless, as if it had always been there. He rechecked the lock, the hinges, the very stones of the cell. Everything was as it should be. A wave of disorientation washed over him. He felt suddenly cold, and strangely lightheaded.

He immediately reported his discovery to Abbot Michael, a man known for his calm demeanor and sharp intellect. The Abbot listened patiently, his brow furrowed with concern. "Show me, Thomas," he said, his voice low and grave. After examining the page, he summoned the other senior monks – Brother Benedict, the monastery’s physician, and Brother Elias, the keeper of records – to witness the anomaly. They, too, were baffled. 

The Abbot decreed that the incident be treated with utmost secrecy. "We must investigate this discreetly," he instructed. "No word of this must leave these walls. Some…unnatural force may be at play.” He ordered Brother Thomas to continue his work, and to be extra vigilant, carefully guarding the manuscript and his own well-being. The unsettling words, “The shadows lengthen, even within stone,” lingered in Thomas’s mind, a cryptic riddle he could not decipher.

Tonight, however, a disquiet settled upon him, a feeling he couldn't quite name.

He'd carefully laid the nearly finished folio to dry on the drying rack, ensuring it was positioned away from the drafty window. It was standard practice; parchment dried slowly, and haste only led to warping and ruined work. Locking the heavy oak door behind him, he’d wished Brother Alaric a good evening, and made his way to the refectory for supper. The scriptorium, as always, was sealed tight from dusk until dawn, the key held by the Abbot himself. No one entered, no one left.

This morning, Thomas had risen early, eager to complete the *Liber Bestiarum* and move on to his next assignment. He’d unlocked the scriptorium, the familiar scent of aged parchment and beeswax assaulting his nostrils, and made his way to the drying rack. That's when he saw it. A new line of text, meticulously penned in an unfamiliar hand, had appeared at the bottom of the folio. It wasn’t his script; he knew his own handwriting intimately. This was different – a smaller, more angular script, the ink a shade darker than his own.

The line read simply: “The river runs red.”

He stared at it, his heart pounding a frantic rhythm against his ribs. Impossible. He’d locked the scriptorium. Brother Alaric had confirmed the lock was secure. There were no other entrances. Agnes kept it locked, the key a heavy, tarnished weight on her keyring. She opened it infrequently, treating the contents with a reverence that bordered on ritual, a way of keeping a piece of him close. The impending arrival of Lord Hoshi, the Shogun’s envoy from Edo, had cast a palpable tension over Silent Bloom, though outwardly, everything appeared pristine. Preparations were frantic, yet executed with a quiet efficiency. Hiroki, Kenji’s apprentice of five years, moved with earnest dedication, polishing the lacquered tea caddies until they gleamed, rearranging the cushions with painstaking care, and vigilantly monitoring the charcoal brazier to ensure a consistent, even heat. He was a diligent student, devoted to his master, but a certain clumsiness clung to him – a slight tremor in his hand when handling delicate porcelain, a tendency to knock against the edge of a table when retrieving a tool.
